intents.title: theBRAIN is native HTML, CSS, JS and JSON

decision.text: Docs, wiki and architecture in theOS/theBRAIN are written as HTML, CSS, JS and JSON. No markdown.
decision.why: One format that the app renders directly, nothing to convert, nothing to drift.

intents.title: Agents act; humans and coops own

decision.text: A signer is a key that signs for an agent. Agents act; only humans and coops own data and agents.
decision.why: Devices come and go; ownership must not move with them.

intents.title: Three kinds of identity: human, coop, agent

decision.text: Identity types: human, coop, agent. Humans and coops own and decide. A coop has roles, named sets of identities that hold humans or coops, never agents or signers; coops may be inside coops, never in a circle. Agents are owned and never in any role; they get policies directly from their owner.
decision.why: Families, teams and organisations are identities of identities; one model covers all of them.

intents.title: Data owns itself: the seal

decision.text: Data is born with a fresh key pair, the seal. Its public key is the data ID. It signs exactly one thing, the first policy, and the private key is wiped.
decision.why: Nobody holds the seal, so it cannot be shared, lost or stolen. Keyhive does the same with its genesis key.

intents.title: One owner per piece of data, and it is an identity

decision.text: The birth record's policy names exactly one owner: an identity, human or coop. The owner may do everything, its policy never expires, and ownership never moves to another identity (AIP-54). The owner is not a role.
decision.why: A role of owners cannot shrink durably: any past owner could revoke the others for good (Keyline's warning). With one owner identity, people change inside the coop, not in the data.

intents.title: Policies go to roles, never to people directly

decision.text: Everyone except the owner gets access through policies. A policy is given to a role (a named set of identities) or, for an identity's own agents, to an agent directly.
decision.why: People come and go; roles stay. Changing who is in a role never touches the data's policies.

intents.title: People see "policies"; underneath they are capabilities

decision.text: The word everyone sees is "policy". Underneath, each policy is a signed capability token that carries its own proof back to the data's birth record and is checked offline.
decision.why: "Policy" is the word ordinary people understand; capabilities are what makes it hold without a server.

intents.title: A policy: role, data, operations, conditions, expiry, proof

decision.text: A policy is a signed certificate with: the role it is given to; the data it applies to; its operations, keyed by name (AIP-56) (create, read, update, delete, want, keep, sync), each optionally narrowed by at (a path), where (matching entries) or a limit; an expiry; the signature of the owner's agent; and the proof chain back to the data's birth record. Identity policies use the same shape with act and own (AIP-48). Writing policies is not an operation: it belongs to the owner (AIP-30).
decision.why: One small vocabulary for content, carrying and the policies themselves. Keyhive's Relay, Read, Edit and Admin map onto it; ours is finer.

intents.title: Sharing only narrows

decision.text: Whoever may share hands on a policy that is the same or smaller: fewer operations, shorter expiry, more conditions. Never more.
decision.why: Attenuation keeps delegation safe without asking anyone. Meadowcap and Biscuit both require each step to sit inside the previous one.

intents.title: Read is encryption, everything else is verification

decision.text: Opening a piece of data at all is enforced by keys; read's conditions by the reader's own engine (AIP-55). Every other operation is enforced by every peer checking each signed change against the policies in the history.
decision.why: Encryption can only be all or nothing per key; signature checks can be as fine as needed.

intents.title: Reading is per piece of data; changes can be as fine as needed

decision.text: Read is granted per piece of data. Anything to be shared on its own is its own data. Create, update and delete can be narrowed to paths and matching entries.
decision.why: A reader holds the plaintext, so finer read limits would be promises, not protection.

intents.title: Every policy expires and renews itself

decision.text: Policies expire after 30 days unless set otherwise. The owner renews unchanged policies a week before they end, under its own policies (a coop can let one agent do renewals). The owner's first policy never expires.
decision.why: Forgotten shares close by themselves; families are never locked out.

intents.title: Endings: revoke and lapse

decision.text: A revoke (by the owner) and a lapse (by any peer that can read the policies, once the date has passed) are the same kind of event in the history. An ending wins over every change that never saw it, turns the data key if the ended policy gave read, and is the delete trigger on honest devices.
decision.why: Validity follows from the history alone, so all copies agree. No clock is trusted.
decision.rejected: Checking expiry against each device's own clock (copies would disagree).

sources.label: Keyhive notebook 06: E2EE in the local-first setting

intents.title: Ambiguity resolves toward less authority

decision.text: When policy, role or ending changes are concurrent with other changes, the result with less authority wins. A change that never saw a removal or an ending is dropped (AIP-13). Nothing wins by being “latest”: order matters only where one change has seen the other, and last-writer-wins is never used for authority (AIP-25). When two holders remove each other at once, both removals stand and the one top repairs (AIP-59).
decision.why: The safe default without a central order. Keyhive's guiding principle.

intents.title: A removed admin means a successor role

decision.text: When an admin is removed from a role, the role is replaced by a successor with a new ID and the remaining members are added again.
decision.why: A removed admin can backdate a revoke by pretending not to have seen their removal. Old revokes then point at a dead role.

intents.title: Keys: identity key, role key, data key

decision.text: Content is encrypted with a data key. The data key is wrapped for the owner and for each reading role. The role key is wrapped for each member's identity key. Each new data key opens the previous one, within the hot window only (AIP-39).
decision.why: Envelope encryption is the proven pattern (HPKE; Keybase teams, Jazz, Cryptree). Removing a member rotates one role key, not every piece of data. Forward secrecy is given up on purpose, because CRDTs need their whole history.

sources.label: Keyhive notebook 06: E2EE in the local-first setting

intents.title: The keyring travels with the data

decision.text: Each piece of data carries its keyring (envelopes, generation, back-links) next to its policies, sealed. An envelope is addressed either to a lock or to another data key (a Value bound to its metadata Doc).
decision.why: No one keeps keys for the data; it is self-contained wherever it goes.

intents.title: Which key turns when

decision.text: Adding a member or giving read: nothing turns. Removing a member: new role key, data keys on next write. Taking read: new data key now. An agent's device stolen: identity key and every role it is in. Concurrent rotations are both kept until the next one.
decision.why: Only read touches keys; the rest is signed policies.

intents.title: Envelopes only for published, signed locks

decision.text: Each agent publishes its own lock (encryption key) in its own history, signed by its signer. Envelopes are made only for locks found there, and only by someone a policy allows.
decision.why: Stops an attacker from slipping in a lock of their own. Closes the gap Keyhive lists as G2.

intents.title: BeeKEM inside large roles, later

decision.text: Small roles use one envelope per reading agent. Roles of several dozen identities and up manage their role key with BeeKEM. Not per piece of data.
decision.why: BeeKEM per document (Keyhive) costs one update per document a removed reader could read; per role it costs one. Every Keyhive crate is pre-alpha and unaudited: pin and audit before use.

intents.title: Data is a Doc or a Value

decision.text: A Doc is JSON that changes, made of CRDT data types (Loro underneath). A Value is bytes that never change, named by the BLAKE3 hash of their sealed bytes (AIP-72), streamed in checked ranges. Every Value has a small metadata Doc; the Value's keyring holds one envelope, addressed to that Doc's data key, so read on the Doc means read on the Value.
decision.why: Mergeable structure where it helps, plain files where it does not.

intents.title: Words: operation, CRDT op

decision.text: An operation is anything you do: what a policy allows and what the engine runs (find, update, want …). A CRDT op is Loro's low-level change, always called “CRDT op”. The slides name CRDT data types, not Loro.
decision.why: One meaning per word.

intents.title: The engine: JSON operations, pluggable, local

decision.text: Every read, change, search and sync is a JSON operation (find, walk, search, near …, and chain, which runs each step under that step's own operation). New kinds plug in and name their broad operation (AIP-53), which a policy must allow. Operations run only on your own device, over what you can read.
decision.why: One engine for everything, with no server in the loop.

intents.title: Peers sync, they never ask

decision.text: No peer ever answers questions about its data for another peer. Peers only carry what policies allow. A shared answer is its own data with its own policy.
decision.why: Removes the trust in the answering device, and the risk of asking one's way to the content.

intents.title: Policies are their own signed set, not a Loro doc

decision.text: Policies, roles and endings are a grow-only set of signed certificates, merged by union and evaluated by our own logic.
decision.why: Policy conflicts need "less authority wins"; Loro's last-writer-wins would resolve them wrongly. Keyhive does the same.

intents.title: Sealed in chunks, linked by hashes

decision.text: Devices seal ranges of changes (Loro update bytes, compressed, then encrypted). Boundaries come from change hashes so every device cuts the same way; small chunks merge into bigger ones over time. Each chunk is hashed and lists the chunks before it; its signed header binds Loro's peer ID to the signer.
decision.why: Sealing op by op makes data huge and uncompressible. Same lesson as Keyhive's sedimentree.

sources.label: Subduction: sync for encrypted history, with iroh transport

intents.title: Carriers see sealed chunks and proofs, never policies

decision.text: Policies are sealed for readers. A carrier checks only proofs: the asker's want proof, and each change author's proof. IDs in proofs are pseudonymous.
decision.why: Keyhive syncs its membership graph to servers in plain text; we keep that private too.

intents.title: Peer to peer over iroh

decision.text: Devices connect directly over iroh: the address is the agent's signer key (AIP-31), relays see only sealed traffic.
decision.why: No cloud in the middle; the address can change without touching the identity.

intents.title: Evaluate Subduction for sync

decision.text: Test Ink & Switch's Subduction (iroh transport, sedimentree, fingerprint sync) before building our own sync.
decision.why: It already syncs encrypted history between peers that cannot read it. Note: current Subduction compares 8-byte fingerprints; RIBLT was in its predecessor Beelay.

sources.label: Subduction: sync for encrypted history, with iroh transport

intents.title: Only the owner changes policies

decision.text: The owner writes and ends all policies on its data; ownership acts (retain, erase, open the archive, migrate to a new schema version) stay with the owner alone. Nobody else writes policies, and ownership is never handed over (AIP-54).
decision.why: Identities work like Gnosis Safes: agents of the identities in its roles sign under the identity's own policies (one signature for now, AIP-49), with one guardian at the top of a coop (AIP-59). So one owner covers several managers, and there is no removed admin who could backdate a revoke.
decision.supersedes: AIP-15; removes admin from the role do-list in AIP-8

intents.title: A signer is the key of an agent

decision.text: A signer is only a key: the current key of exactly one agent identity, registered in that agent's history. How it is kept is up to the device the agent runs on: derived from the passkey's PRF plus a per-device salt on phones, the keychain on laptops, an environment variable, secret manager or HSM on servers. Loro's peer ID stays a number, bound to the signer in each chunk's signed header.
decision.why: Separates who acts (identities) from what signs (keys). Not derived from the passkey alone: synced passkeys give several devices the same secret, and Apple's Secure Enclave holds only P-256 keys.
decision.supersedes: the separate iroh key in AIP-28

intents.title: Words, and dialing identities

decision.text: Agents sign for the identity that owns them; roles are sets of identities; data is acted upon. Peers dial identities: each identity publishes a signed record of its agents, each agent's history holds its current address (its signer's public key), and the connection goes to whichever agent is online.
decision.why: One word per thing. Addressing identities keeps the address stable while signers change, like a phone number and its SIM.

intents.title: Sealed chunks settle in layers (sedimentree)

decision.text: Each sealed change is hashed (BLAKE3). Its leading zero bytes give its depth; a change of depth 1 or more closes a chunk with everything since the last one at that depth. Deeper chunks hold shallower ones. Equal content gives an equal minimal hash.
decision.why: Every peer, even one that reads nothing, cuts the same chunks; old history becomes a few big chunks; equality is one hash.

intents.title: Fingerprints inside data, RIBLT across data

decision.text: Inside one piece of data, peers compare 8-byte keyed fingerprints of its layers and swap the missing sealed chunks in 1.5 round trips. Across many pieces of data, peers use RIBLT set reconciliation to find which ones differ.
decision.why: Sedimentree keeps the count inside one piece small, so fingerprints are cheap there; across thousands, RIBLT costs about 1.5 summaries per difference, whatever the total.

sources.label: Subduction design: batch sync with fingerprints

intents.title: Compact at stable points; newcomers get snapshots

decision.text: When every writer has seen a version, a device may cut there: newcomers get a snapshot plus the ops after it, never the old history. What lies before the cut is sealed under a new key; honest devices drop the old chunks and keys.
decision.why: CRDT history keeps deleted text and needs old keys, so forward secrecy is lost. Cutting at stable points gives it back for everything before the cut, without losing any late op.

sources.label: Keyhive notebook 06: E2EE in the local-first setting

intents.title: Heal: keys turn regularly

decision.text: Role keys and data keys turn regularly, not only when someone leaves, so a stolen key soon opens nothing new (post-compromise security). Forgetting the past is AIP-39; the archive is AIP-40.
decision.why: Full forward secrecy for live CRDT history is impossible: a late op may need any old state. Keyhive gave forward secrecy up; BeeKEM's κ parameter shows the trade-off. These three layers get as close as the setting allows.

sources.label: Keyhive notebook 06: E2EE in the local-first setting

intents.title: Lock away: older keys behind a fresh tap

decision.text: Current keys stay ready on the device. Older keys, needed only for scrolling far back or merging a very late CRDT op, are sealed under an archive key derived from the passkey's PRF secret. The secure hardware releases it only after a fresh tap or face scan; afterwards it is wiped from memory.
decision.why: A thief with the device, or malware reading app storage, gets only the current keys. Limits: malware running during the tap, or a taken-over passkey sync account.

intents.title: Signing policies are pluggable

decision.text: Each identity's signing policies hold one entry per action, built from kinds: threshold (k of n), weights, all-of / any-of, time lock with objection window. A policy kind is identified by the hash of its specification and is declarative data, not code. A device that does not know a kind treats the policy as not satisfied. Changing the signing policies needs the policy for that action.
decision.why: New kinds of signing policies can be added over time without old devices ever wrongly accepting something.

intents.title: Keys live hot, then cold, and can be erased

decision.text: Hot: the newest keys, linked by back-links and ready on readers' devices; they turn regularly (AIP-36). Cold: at rotation boundaries older than the hot window, the chain is cut; older keys leave the chain and go to the owner's archive. Erased: on request, keys are shredded everywhere. Late writers from before a cut lose and get a conflict view of what was not adopted. The hot window is 30 days, equal to a policy's lifetime.
decision.why: Back-links and an archive cannot coexist for the same keys: a stolen current key would open the whole past. Splitting by age gives heal, archive and erasure one consistent lifecycle.

sources.label: Keyhive notebook 06: E2EE in the local-first setting

intents.title: The archive belongs to the owner identity

decision.text: Cold keys are sealed to the owner's archive key, which is itself sealed to the locks of the owner's agents that hold own (for a coop: the agents acting for it with own, AIP-57). Opening the archive follows the owner's own policies. The archive key is not tied to one device. A device may add a local tap as convenience, not as protection.
decision.why: The identity owns, never a signer (AIP-2). Ownership of the past follows the same policies as ownership of the present.

intents.title: Words: archive and retain

decision.text: Archive is the normal cold storage of old keys and history. Retain is legal long-term keeping, for a set period.
decision.why: Two different promises, two words.

intents.title: Erase: delete, cut, shred

decision.text: To erase personal data from any Doc: delete it normally, cut a fresh snapshot without it under a new key, and shred the keys of every chunk before the cut on all honest devices and in the archive; carriers drop those chunks. Works on any text, with no need to plan per piece of data. The history before the cut is lost.
decision.why: Tombstones keep no content in the live state; the content lives only in old sealed chunks, so destroying their keys erases it (crypto-shredding). Splitting personal data into its own pieces does not scale.
decision.rejected: Personal data as separate erasable pieces of data (does not work for a text naming ten people).

intents.title: Retain: an owner event at any time

decision.text: The owner can say “retain until <date>” at any time; the date can only move later. Until then, honest devices refuse cuts, shreds and erasure. A retention role names identities that keep the sealed bytes (want, keep) and may hold an envelope of the archive key. Stored as canonical CBOR, exported as JSON and PDF/A, resealed periodically under current algorithms.
decision.why: Bookkeeping must be kept for years (in Germany 10 years for books, 8 for vouchers since 2025; check with a tax adviser), and a legal retention duty takes priority over erasure (GDPR Art. 17(3)(b)).

intents.title: An identity's policies and data policies never overlap

decision.text: An identity's own policies answer who speaks for it: policies on the identity, given to its roles or its own agents, with act and own; conditions may name which data an agent acts on. A piece of data's policies answer what an identity may do with it: policies on the data, given to roles, with data operations. Signature counts appear only on identity policies (AIP-48, AIP-49). A change is valid only if both hold. A coop is like a small DAO: roles, a guardian, assets, nesting.
decision.why: Agency and access are different questions; mixing them made the coop example ambiguous.

intents.title: Canonical CBOR for everything signed or hashed

decision.text: Everything that is signed, hashed or stored uses canonical CBOR (RFC 8949 deterministic encoding). Everything people read is JSON or PDF/A.
decision.why: Same data, same bytes, same hash and signature; JSON has no canonical form. CBOR carries keys, hashes and signatures as raw bytes, keeps JSON's data model, and is what WebAuthn and COSE already use.

intents.title: Agents: owned by one human or coop, acting by its policies

decision.text: An agent identity (phone, laptop, watch, server, AI assistant) is owned by exactly one human or coop and acts only through policies its owner gives it: who = the agent, on what = the owner, operations act / own / govern, with conditions (which data, limits, expiry). The owner and its first agent are born together in one record signed by the agent's key. Losing a device means revoking its agent's policy.
decision.why: Devices are owned, not members; acting on behalf is delegation by policies (AIP-48). One genesis record removes the chicken-and-egg problem.
decision.supersedes: the earlier “device is a member of” model

intents.title: Policy-writing is delegated through share, narrowing only

decision.text: A role holding share may write policies for other roles, but only within its own operations, conditions and expiry; it may end only policies it issued itself; when its own policy ends, every policy issued under it ends too (cascade); writes by a removed delegate that never saw the ending are dropped. The owner's policies are the root and never fall this way.
decision.why: Gives teams day-to-day delegation without the problems of admin roles: no granting more than you hold, no policy wars between delegates, no backdated revokes.

intents.title: One policy shape, one plugin system

decision.text: Every policy has one shape: who, on what, operations, conditions, expiry. An identity's policies have one of its roles or one of its own agents as who and the identity itself as target, with operations act and own. A piece of data's policies have a role as who and the data as target. Operations and conditions (at, where, limit …; later signature counts, AIP-49) are plugins in one registry, each named by the hash of its specification, declarative, failing closed when unknown. Each condition plugin declares which target it may be used on, so signature conditions stay on identities (AIP-44).
decision.why: One language and one engine for all policies, with the separation between agency and access kept by the target.

intents.title: One signature by default; counts come later as plugins

decision.text: For now, every act and own of an identity needs one signature from an agent acting under the identity's policies: its own agent, or an agent of an identity in one of its roles (1 of 1). Behind them stands the identity's one guardian (AIP-91). Signature counts (k of n), weights and waiting times are not part of the first version; they are added later as condition plugins (AIP-48), and devices that do not know them treat them as not satisfied.
decision.why: Keeps the first version simple while the plugin system leaves room to grow.

intents.title: Record conventions

decision.text: Every stored or sent thing is a record: {"type": <schema ref of its kind>, …fields, "after", "seq", "sig"} (AIP-90) in canonical CBOR (shown as JSON), decoded strictly; examples omit after and seq except where they matter (AIP-61). IDs are typed: human:, coop:, agent:, data:, role:, policy:, ending: and chunk: followed by b3: and the BLAKE3 hash of the record without its signature; value: b3: is the hash of the bytes. A #label after an ID is only for people (human:b3:q4x7…#you). A birth record (genesis) holds a random nonce or the keys it creates, so no two share an ID. A record cannot contain its own hash, so inside a birth record the identities it creates are named by kind (“this human”, “this agent”); their IDs are b3(kind ‖ record). One genesis record can create a human or coop and its first agent. A schema is pinned as its data ID, @ and the hash of the frozen version (AIP-66): data:b3:Sc4…@b3:1f0…#todo-list. Public keys: ed25519:… (signers), x25519:… (locks). Secret keys never appear; they are named, for example datakey:house-list/3. CRDT op IDs are Loro's peer and counter (5f3a9c:41). Times are RFC 3339 in UTC. Signatures: "sig": {"by": agent ID, "key": ed25519 public key, "value": …}; every record is signed by an agent, except guardian acts, which are signed by a guardian key (AIP-91). A proof is the ordered list of record IDs from a birth record to the acting agent; examples always show a policy's proof. Record kinds: genesis, identity, role, policy, renewal, ending, envelope, keyring, change, chunk, value, meta, retain, erase, directory, proof, want, news, operation, lens, migration. Lenses and migrations have lens: and migration: IDs. Identity policies do not expire unless they say so.
decision.why: Slides and code use the same shapes and names, so the examples are drafts of the real schema, not illustrations.

intents.title: Only roles and policies; no members

decision.text: There are no membership records. A role is a named set of identities; a policy says what a role (or an agent) may do on an identity or a piece of data. A coop has no members, only roles; policies on the coop say what each role may do, for example act and own for a home's “family”, only act for a street's “homes”; the coop's guardian is its root (AIP-91), and may give own to a role so its holders manage roles and policies.
decision.why: One mechanism for everything: who is in which group (roles) and what that group may do (policies).
decision.supersedes: membership as its own record kind

intents.title: No data without a schema

decision.text: Every piece of data names a schema in its genesis; a Value's metadata Doc names one for the Value and one for itself. A schema is a JSON Schema stored as a Loro Doc with its own birth record, owner and policies. Data pins an exact schema version (the hash of the schema Doc's state); moving to a new version is an owner's change. Every peer validates every change against the schema and drops what does not fit. Paths (JSON Pointer, * for any index or key) give every part of the data an address for policies and operations.
decision.why: Typed data makes policies and operations precise and keeps every copy well-formed without a server.

intents.title: Engine operations are specific and typed

decision.text: Policies name broad operations (read, create, update, delete, want, keep, sync). Engine operations are specific and each belongs to one: read → get, find, walk, search, near, count; create → create, insert; update → set, move, splice; delete → remove, delete; chain runs each step under that step's own operation. Every operation names data, schema version and path; the engine validates its input against the plugin's shape and the schema before running it.
decision.why: Precise, checkable operations, with policies that stay short and readable.

intents.title: Only the owner writes policies: no passing on, no hand-over yet

decision.text: Only the owner writes and ends policies on its data, through its own agents. No role can pass a policy on (there is no share operation), and ownership is never handed over: whoever needs to work on the data gets a policy. Delegated, narrowing-only policy-writing may come back later as its own decision.
decision.why: One author for a piece of data's policies keeps every check simple: no cascades, no revokes by other issuers, no backdating by a removed delegate. Policies already cover everything a hand-over would.
decision.rejected: Share with attenuation and cascading ends (AIP-9, AIP-47), for now.

intents.title: Read is an operation like any other

decision.text: Read carries the same conditions as every other operation (at, where, limit) and covers specific engine operations (get, find, walk, search, near, count). The data key opens a whole piece of data, so read's conditions are kept by the reader's own engine on honest devices; anything that must stay unseen is its own data, with its own key. Changes are checked by every peer.
decision.why: One query logic for every operation: a policy always says what, where and how much. Keys still mark the hard boundary of what can be opened at all.

intents.title: One operation shape everywhere

decision.text: Policies write operations as one object keyed by operation name: {"read": {"at": "/items"}, "create": {"at": "/items", "limit": 20}}, defined once as a schema. Each name appears once; its value holds the conditions: at (a JSON Pointer or a list of them, default "" = the whole data or identity), where and limit, which only narrow. The engine's record (its operation record) uses the same fields for one specific operation (find, set …). An engine operation is allowed when a policy names its broad operation, its path lies under at, and where and limit hold. The Operations object is one recursive schema: on an identity policy, act's data condition maps data IDs to Operations objects, so data policies, agent scopes and engine operations share it.
decision.why: One source of truth for what an operation is: no repeated keys, no bare names next to objects, and every example, record and check reads the same fields.

sources.label: Meadowcap (areas: path prefixes that only narrow)

intents.title: Keys follow agents: no shared identity key

decision.text: There is no key shared by all of an identity's agents. Each agent has its own lock, published in its own history (AIP-19). A data key is sealed to the role keys of the roles that may read it and to the locks of the owner's agents whose policies cover reading it; a role key is sealed to the locks of the agents of each identity in the role whose policies cover reading for that identity. So an agent gets exactly the keys both layers give it: the data's policies (which identity may read) and the identity's policies (which of its agents reads for it, AIP-58). Carriers get none. Any current reader that has seen a change in the reader set may turn a key; every peer checks that envelopes go only to current readers. When two key turns are concurrent, the next key is sealed only to the readers both allowed, and nobody encrypts under a generation older than an ending it knows. Adding someone: envelopes for their reading agents; a newcomer starts from today's snapshot unless the owner opens older history. Removing someone or losing an agent: it gets nothing new, and every role key and data key it could open turns (role keys now, data keys on the next write; data keys now when read is taken).
decision.why: Reading must follow the same delegation as writing: a watch limited to health data, or a backup with only want and keep, must not be able to decrypt everything, and removing someone from a coop's role must stop their reading without a cascade of identity-key turns. Keyhive does the same: every individual with Read is a leaf of the key tree, one with only Relay is not.

intents.title: An agent has two parts: who it is, and what it may do

decision.text: An agent is its own identity, owned by exactly one human or coop, with its own signer; on phones the signer is derived from the passkey, which is the single source of truth for now (stolen devices and recovery are out of scope). Owning an agent gives it nothing. What it may do comes only from policies on the identity it acts for, given by that identity: your phone gets act and own on you; a coop's always-on server gets act on the coop only to carry one list. Act's one condition is data: a map from data ID to an ordinary Operations object (AIP-56), conditions included: {"act": {"data": {"data:b3:7Hq…#house-list": {"want": {}, "keep": {}}}}}. Without data, act covers all of the owner's data. Agents are never in roles and never get data policies; data policies go to roles of humans and coops (AIP-6, AIP-44). A change or a read is allowed only if both layers allow it. A policy belongs to the identity that gave it, not to the agent that signed it; it ends only by that identity's ending or its expiry. The owner and its first agent are born together in one record. Acting for an identity is a chain of policies, one per hop: an agent acts for its owner; an identity acts for a coop through the coop's policy to a role that lists it; the chain is as long as needed (phone → you → home → street; home's server → home). Agent policies on an identity are written by that identity's guardian (AIP-70).
decision.why: Two clean layers: who speaks for an identity, and what an identity may do with data. The same two layers decide which keys an agent gets (AIP-57).

intents.title: One top: one owner per piece of data, one guardian per coop

decision.text: Authority has exactly one top and flows only downward: a piece of data has one owner (AIP-5), and every identity has one guardian (AIP-91). Nobody can give more than it holds, and nobody below can touch the guardian. When two holders below the top remove each other at the same moment, both removals stand and the guardian repairs, for example by adding one back; there is no seniority and no coin flip. The top cannot clash with itself because it is one.
decision.why: Without a total order, peers with equal power can remove each other at once and leave nobody, and with one signature anyone in a coop's role could take it over. Keyhive's Keyline calls this mutual destruction in the root role; its mitigation is a single owner at the top, with every layer below repairable from above. Gnosis Safes avoid it with a blockchain's total order, which a local-first system does not have.

intents.title: Only the owner ends policies; expiry is checked on every change

learn.concept: Do endings hold?

scenarios.scenario: A backdated write in the same history
scenarios.why: A change that leaves the ending out of after counts as concurrent with it, and the ending wins over the ended holder.

decision.text: Every change carries the time its author signed it and counts only if that time is before the expiry of the policy it relies on; devices reject times far ahead of their own clock. Only the owner's agents write endings into the history: a revoke at any time, a lapse once the date has passed. An ending drops only the ended holder's own changes that it did not list as seen (AIP-61), never anyone else's. Policies expire after 30 days unless set otherwise; the owner renews unchanged policies a week before they end, and a renewal names the policy it renews, so ending one ends the chain. renew is its own operation, so a coop can give one always-on agent only that job. Other peers may stop handing out keys and chunks once a date has passed by their own clock: a local choice, never written into the history. An owner who is offline never causes a wipe. An ending turns the data key if the ended policy gave read, and is the delete trigger on honest devices.
decision.why: If any reader could write a lapse, a fast clock would end policies early, and a lapse claiming to have seen nothing would drop weeks of everyone's work. Keyhive has no expiry for this reason; Willow checks each entry's own timestamp. We combine both: per-change time checks, and endings only from the owner.

intents.title: Every record says what it had seen

decision.text: Every signed record carries after (the latest changes its author had seen of the data, of the policy set and of each identity in its proof) and seq (its signer's running number). “Saw it” means listed in after, directly or through what those records saw. A list counts only for its author's own authority: nobody can make another signer's ending disappear by leaving it out. Two different records with the same signer and seq prove the signer lied: both are invalid.
decision.why: Endings, removals and “less authority wins” depend on what came before what; without it in the record, “never saw it” is undefined. Keyhive's revocations record the content heads their issuer had seen for the same reason.

intents.title: History keeps everything; what you see is computed

decision.text: No change is ever removed from the sealed history. What you see is computed: the valid changes always form one causally complete version, which every device computes the same way and Loro can open. An ending invalidates the ended holder's own changes that it did not see, and with them every change built on them. Honest changes that fell only because they built on an invalid one come back to their authors as a conflict view, and their devices apply them again as new changes, as for late writers after a cut (AIP-39). The next cut removes invalid changes for good.
decision.why: An op-based CRDT cannot skip an operation: Loro keeps a change whose dependencies are missing as pending. Keyhive lists what happens to a revoked writer's content as an open question (whiteout).

intents.title: One writer can't make devices disagree

decision.text: A change's Loro peer ID is derived from its agent, epoch and data ID (AIP-69), so nobody can write under another's ID. Two different changes with the same peer and counter prove the signer lied: both are invalid and its policy is ended. On arrival, each change is checked on its own: signature, policy, the schema's shape. Rules that span concurrent changes (limits, required entries across a list, loops of coops inside coops) are settled when the view is built, in one fixed order (causal order, then hash). A change that uses an unknown plugin waits until the plugin is known; it is not rejected.
decision.why: Otherwise one authorised writer could split devices for good: by signing two versions of one change, by two changes that are valid alone but not together, or by a plugin old devices don't know.

intents.title: Data is named by the hash of its birth record

decision.text: A piece of data is born with a birth record: its schema, its first policy naming the owner (own, no expiry) and a random nonce, signed by an agent acting for the owner with own. The data ID is data:b3: and the BLAKE3 hash of the record without its signature. There is no seal: nothing has to be kept or destroyed, and a second birth record is simply different data. A proof starts at a birth record, whose ID names it. New data born inside another piece of data (an item of a list) is born under the parent's create policy and follows the parent's owner and policies by link.
decision.why: A data ID that is a key's public half trusts the creator to destroy the key; one who keeps it can sign a second birth and become a second owner. Keyhive warns of the same: a retained subject key can re-root a document. Naming by hash is what AIP-50 already does for identities.

intents.title: Carriers see who may carry, never what is inside

decision.text: The policies, roles and endings of a piece of data are signed but not encrypted for the peers that carry it, with pseudonymous IDs; content and keyrings stay sealed. A carrier checks every want against them and learns endings, so it stops serving an ended holder. A want is signed over the carrier's fresh challenge, so it cannot be replayed elsewhere. Peers forward news and run set summaries only for data both sides may want. What a carrier learns is stated plainly: chunk hashes, sizes and links, the signing agents, who may carry and read the data (pseudonymously), and when it changes. A relay (AIP-28) is different: it only forwards encrypted packets between two devices and holds nothing.
decision.why: A carrier cannot check proofs against policies it cannot see, nor stop serving a revoked holder if endings are hidden from it. Keyhive's relays see the membership graph for the same reason and list it as unprotected metadata.

intents.title: Schema versions are frozen and travel with the data

decision.text: Every piece of data names a schema version in its birth record; a Value's metadata Doc names one for the Value and one for itself. A schema is a JSON Schema edited as a Loro Doc with its own birth record, owner and policies. Each published version is frozen: its ID is the BLAKE3 hash of its canonical CBOR, and the frozen version is a Value carried with every piece of data that pins it, so no schema owner can take it away. Every change names the version it was written in and is checked against that version; a change naming a version or lens a device doesn't have yet waits. Paths (JSON Pointer, * for any index or key) give every part of the data an address for policies and operations. Every reference to a schema, a plugin's specification or input shape, or the registry of operation names is a data ID with @ and a version hash; never a bare name. The #label after it is only for people.
decision.why: A live schema Doc read under its owner's policies would let that owner block every list that uses it, and a Loro state has no content hash to pin. Frozen, carried versions fix both.

intents.title: Lenses between versions; moving on rewrites nothing

decision.text: A new version comes with a lens: a list of operations (rename, add with a default, remove with a value for old readers, copy, convert by registered two-way conversions, wrap, hoist) that runs both ways, is named by its hash and can be checked by anyone: applied to the old version it must give exactly the new one. Ambiguous lenses are refused. Each version maps its paths to stored keys; a rename keeps the stored key, an added field gets a new one, a removed field's key stays. The owner moves the data to a new version with one signed migration record (an ownership act, AIP-30) that rewrites nothing; the data then accepts changes in every version along its lenses, until the owner retires one. Every device merges first, then projects the merged state along the lens path (shortest, ties to the smaller lens ID) into its own version. Policies and operations name the version their paths use; the data is projected into that version, and policies are never translated. Two concurrent migrations both stand until the owner writes a version with a lens from each.
decision.why: Old and new apps keep working on the same data at the same time, with no flag day and nothing rewritten. Jazz 2 and Cambria show the shape; stored keys make it fit a CRDT, where Cambria's op-by-op translation on Automerge was abandoned.

intents.title: Breaking changes go through a Loro branch

decision.text: A change that a lens cannot run both ways (splitting a field, a list becoming a map) is a rewrite. The owner's agent takes the frontier F of the valid view, forks the Doc at F (fork_at), applies the lens there and takes the diff; on the main Doc it checks out F, edits detached under its derived peer ID (AIP-63), applies the diff and commits one change that depends on F, signed with a migration record. Ops made on the fork are never signed. Every peer verifies by repeating the rewrite at F; a mismatch is dropped. Old-version changes that never saw the rewrite go back to their authors, who apply them again through the lens (AIP-62). A total break starts a successor instead (AIP-71).
decision.why: Loro has no branch object, but fork_at, checkout and apply_diff give a deterministic branch-and-merge that every peer can recompute, so nobody has to trust the migrating device.

intents.title: Joining by invite; agent epochs

learn.concept: Agents: who it is, and what it may do
learn.weakness: An honest restore from a backup currently looks like a lying signer (AIP-61, AIP-63), and pairing needs a manual exchange with one specific agent online.
strengths: Every device is its own identity with its own scope; most systems give all devices one key (Classic Jazz shares one agent secret, Holochain has one key per app, Keet attests devices without scopes).
elsewhere: Urbit: every point carries a key revision (life) and a continuity number (rift); traffic under an old revision fails.
Holepunch blind-pairing and Autopass: a one-time invite key with an expiry, answered by any online member.
Keet: a root key re-bootstraps with a new epoch; verifiers reject proofs from older epochs.

scenarios.scenario: A signer that lies (two records, one number)
scenarios.why: Caught only where both records meet; if both become invalid, a signer could void a record it regrets; an honest restore looks the same.
scenarios.fix: Warrants carried by carriers; a lie never voids an ending; a restore starts a new epoch.

proposal.text: Every agent record header names its signer revision and a continuity epoch; a restored or reinstalled device starts a new epoch, so it never reuses a running number or a CRDT op ID. New agents pair through invite records: a one-time key, an expiry and the agent policy it will create, written into the identity's history so any of its agents with govern can answer.
proposal.why: An honest restore from a backup currently looks like a lying signer (AIP-61, AIP-63), and pairing needs a manual exchange with one specific agent online.

decision.text: A new agent joins by invite. The guardian, or an agent with own, writes an invite record into the identity's history: a one-time public key, a short expiry and exactly the operations the new agent gets, within its own. The one-time secret goes to the new device out of band (QR code or typed code). The new device makes its own signer and lock and signs its birth record, which names the invite and carries a second signature by the one-time key. That pair is the new agent's policy, exactly as granted: no other agent has to be online. An invite is single use: two births citing it are both invalid; the owner may end an unused invite. Every agent record carries rev (signer revision) and epoch (continuity epoch); a restored or reinstalled device writes an epoch record and starts a new epoch, so it never reuses a running number or a CRDT op ID.
decision.why: Pairing needs no second device online and can't be widened by the new device; a copied code is worthless after one use or its expiry. An honest restore no longer looks like a lying signer.

intents.title: One guardian per identity, changed only by succession

learn.concept: One top: one guardian per coop
learn.weakness: With one guardian, every change of roles or guardianship waits for one person's devices.
strengths: No two equals at the top, so no mutual destruction (Keyhive's Keyline: a single-owner root role has no duel).
Matches Matrix room version 12, where creators cannot be demoted, and avoids the coin flips of Autopass and Secure Scuttlebutt.
elsewhere: NextGraph puts removals behind a threshold signature of a quorum.
Hypercore manifests name signers and a quorum.
Gnosis Safe: k of n owners, ordered by a chain.

proposal.text: The guardian role stays the one top (AIP-59). When signature counts arrive (AIP-49), govern becomes k of n inside that role, so the rule stays “one top”. Until then a guardian names its successor in a signed succession record before leaving.
proposal.why: With one guardian, every change of roles or governance waits for one person's devices.

decision.text: Every human and every coop has exactly one guardian, the one top of its authority, which alone holds govern on it. A human is its own guardian and acts as one through its own agents with govern (passkeys are the single source of truth for now). A coop's guardian is its guardian role, which always holds exactly one identity. A coop's guardian changes only by succession: the current guardian signs a new guardian role record naming its successor, which must list the previous one as seen. A guardian can't leave or be removed without naming a successor, so no coop ends up without one. If two guardian role records are concurrent (the guardian's own agents disagreed), neither takes effect until a record sees both. Agents have no guardian; their owner governs them. Below the guardian, concurrent removals both stand and the guardian repairs (AIP-59). Several guardians acting by majority, with chained signatures, may come later. The guardian exercises govern through its own chain (your phone → you → the coop); a coop's own agents never hold govern on it.
decision.why: Keeps one top, so no two equals can remove each other at once and a coop can never lock itself out, without signature counts or quorums yet. The word guardian says what the role is for: keeping the coop whole.

intents.title: Successors: data that continues other data

learn.concept: Data named by the hash of its birth record
learn.weakness: Data named by its birth record has no way to continue under a new one.
strengths: Self-certifying, with no key to keep or destroy; Matrix v12 names rooms the same way, and a Hypercore's key is the hash of its manifest.
elsewhere: Hypercore's prologue lets a log under new signers continue verifiable history.
Holochain's CloseChain and OpenChain link an old chain to its successor.

proposal.text: New data may name a predecessor in its birth record (data ID and frontier hash), and the old data gets a signed forward link from its owner. This is the path for total schema breaks and any future change of owner.
proposal.why: Data named by its birth record has no way to continue under a new one.

decision.text: Data may continue as new data. The owner starts new data whose birth record names a predecessor (the old data ID and the hash of the old valid view's frontier) and signs a successor record on the old data naming the new data, the same frontier and, if the schema changes, a lens. A succession holds only if both name each other with the same frontier. Old and new have the same owner; succession never moves ownership (AIP-54). Data has at most one successor; two concurrent successor records both fail until one sees the other. The new data's first state equals the old valid view at the frontier, through the lens if given, and every peer can recompute it. The successor record ends every create, update and delete on the old data; read, want and keep stay until ended separately. Changes on the old data that didn't see the successor record go back to their authors as a conflict view, to be applied again on the successor (AIP-62). Links to old data resolve forward through the chain.
decision.why: A clean way out for breaks too big even for a branch (AIP-68), checkable by everyone, without hand-over and without rewriting history. Hypercore's prologue and Holochain's CloseChain/OpenChain do the same for logs and chains.

intents.title: Values named by the hash of their sealed bytes

learn.concept: Values named by the hash of their plaintext
learn.weakness: Carriers can't check a plaintext hash, and the name lets anyone confirm that you hold a file they know.
strengths: Global deduplication; streams in verified ranges.
elsewhere: Hypercore builds its Merkle tree over ciphertext; iroh-blobs verifies BLAKE3 of the stored bytes.

proposal.text: Sealed Values are stored and named by the BLAKE3 hash of their ciphertext; the plaintext hash appears only inside the sealed metadata Doc. Encryption runs in segments aligned to iroh-blobs' 16 KiB groups, so ranges stay decryptable.
proposal.why: Carriers can't check a plaintext hash, and the name lets anyone confirm that you hold a file they know.

decision.text: A Value is sealed before it is named: its plaintext is cut into 16 KiB segments, aligned to iroh-blobs' chunk groups, and each segment is sealed with the Value's own fresh key (XChaCha20-Poly1305) and a nonce derived from its index. The Value's ID is the BLAKE3 root over the sealed bytes, so carriers and readers verify every range against it. The plaintext's hash appears only inside the sealed metadata Doc, never in a name, a want or a news record. There is no convergent encryption: equal files sealed twice get different names.
decision.why: Carriers can't check a plaintext hash, and the name lets anyone confirm that you hold a file they know.

intents.title: Acknowledged finality and owner checkpoints

learn.concept: History keeps everything; the view is computed
learn.weakness: Without finality, a late ending can unwind arbitrarily old changes built on the ended holder's.
strengths: The same shape as Autobase: a deterministic view over a causal graph, rebuilt when it reorders, but without a quorum of indexers.
elsewhere: Autobase: order becomes final once a majority of indexers has signed it (signedLength).
Loro's mergeable containers converge on one ID for containers created at a fixed key.
Urbit Clay's join and mash: re-apply cleanly where possible, annotate otherwise.

proposal.text: Every record's after is an acknowledgement. Once every current reader, or the owner in a signed checkpoint, has acknowledged a frontier, it is final: nothing before it is evaluated again, cuts and compaction start there instead of at a clock age, and a record that claims to change the final past proves its signer lied.
proposal.why: Without finality, a late ending can unwind arbitrarily old changes built on the ended holder's.

intents.title: Lens properties, version negotiation, retiring versions

learn.concept: Frozen versions, lenses, breaking changes through a branch
learn.weakness: Peers must carry every version in use, with no way to retire one, and nothing checks lenses beyond their shape.
strengths: Goes further than the others: Jazz 2's lenses rely on one central sequencer and an admin-only catalogue; Cambria's op-by-op translation on Automerge was abandoned; Hyperschema allows only additive changes; Holochain starts a new network for every rule change; Urbit marks convert per ship.
elsewhere: Jazz 2: translate-then-apply must equal apply-then-translate (INV-LENS-14).
Hyperschema: an additive-only rule, checked mechanically.
Urbit: a published mark's type never changes (discipline); peers negotiate versions.

proposal.text: Every lens gets property tests in the shape of Jazz's INV-LENS-14 (translate then apply equals apply then translate). Versions that need no rewrite pass an additive-only check. Peers exchange the versions they speak at the start of sync. The owner retires a version with an ending.
proposal.why: Peers must carry every version in use, with no way to retire one, and nothing checks lenses beyond their shape.

intents.title: Limits counted per author; no remote queries in iroh-blobs

learn.concept: Local, typed engine operations; limits across changes
learn.weakness: A limit settled when the view is built can flip changes that were already accepted, and Observe is a remote query against AIP-24.
strengths: Peers never answer each other's queries (AIP-24): no remote answerer to trust.
elsewhere: Holochain rate-limits along the author's own chain, checkable on arrival.
Jazz caches query results per schema version.

proposal.text: Limits such as “20 items” count along each author's own running number, so they are checked on arrival and never flip. iroh-blobs' Observe is disabled except for the owner's agents. Query results are cached per schema version.
proposal.why: A limit settled when the view is built can flip changes that were already accepted, and Observe is a remote query against AIP-24.

intents.title: Role deltas, invites, and writes imply read

learn.concept: Owner-only policies and roles
learn.weakness: Full role lists lose unrelated concurrent adds, a revoke concurrent with a renewal is unspecified, every join needs the owner online, and a writer without the data key can't encrypt.
strengths: No delegation, so no cascades and no backdating by a removed delegate, the problems Keyhive and p2panda solve with heavy machinery.
elsewhere: p2panda: membership as add and remove operations; a removal beats a concurrent re-add of the same member only.
Tlon: invite tokens with an expiry and limited claims.
Classic Jazz: a writeOnly role with per-writer write keys sealed to readers.
Meadowcap: a capability names a receiver key whose possession is proven per session.

scenarios.scenario: Removal and re-add at the same moment
scenarios.why: Removal wins (AIP-14). With role records as full lists, an unrelated add at the same moment is lost too.
scenarios.fix: Role records as add and remove deltas; a removal beats a concurrent add of the same identity only.

scenarios.scenario: A revoke at the same moment as a renewal
scenarios.why: Unspecified: the renewal is a new policy the revoke doesn't name.
scenarios.fix: A revoke beats a concurrent renewal of the same policy; a renewal names what it renews (AIP-60).

proposal.text: Role records become add and remove deltas; a removal beats a concurrent add of the same identity, and nothing else. A revoke beats a concurrent renewal of the same policy. The owner can sign invite records (“whoever presents this one-time key may join role R until T”), so joining needs no owner online. Create, update and delete on content require read; write-only comes later with write keys.
proposal.why: Full role lists lose unrelated concurrent adds, a revoke concurrent with a renewal is unspecified, every join needs the owner online, and a writer without the data key can't encrypt.

intents.title: Signer hash chains; endings name chain heads

learn.concept: Backdating across histories
learn.weakness: Critical: an ending in another history (an agent revoked on its human, a member removed from a coop) can't be listed by the data's records, so backdated changes slip in.
strengths: Within one piece of data, “never saw it” is now defined and checked (AIP-61).
elsewhere: Keybase orders all chains through the server's Merkle root; Anytype through a consensus node; NextGraph through a quorum; Peergos through a pointer server. No system reviewed stops cross-history backdating without such a point.
KERI and Keybase: each signer's records form a hash chain (running number plus previous hash).

scenarios.scenario: A backdated write across histories (an agent revoked on its human; an identity removed from the home's role, writing on street data)
scenarios.why: The data's records can't list an ending that lives in another history, so a change citing the old identity head passes.
scenarios.fix: Signer hash chains; every ending names the ended signer's chain head; non-ancestors drop on all data.

scenarios.why: A proof crosses three histories; the same gap as backdating across histories.
scenarios.fix: As above: chain heads in every ending.

proposal.text: Every signer's records form a hash chain (running number plus previous hash); chain headers travel without content. Every ending or removal names the ended signer's chain head, and records that are not ancestors of that head are dropped on all data. The owner, the one top, is the linearisation point for its own authority.
proposal.why: Critical: an ending in another history (an agent revoked on its human, an identity removed from a coop's role) can't be listed by the data's records, so backdated changes slip in.

intents.title: Lies freeze the signer; warrants

learn.concept: Lying signers and their proof
learn.weakness: As written, both conflicting records become invalid, which a signer could use to void a record it regrets.
strengths: Two records with the same signer and number are caught.
elsewhere: Hypercore: two signed roots for one length freeze the log and are a proof anyone can pass on.
Holochain: signed warrants, re-checked and gossiped, block the author.
p2panda's resolver tests cover mutual and nested removals.

scenarios.scenario: A signer that lies (two records, one number)
scenarios.why: Caught only where both records meet; if both become invalid, a signer could void a record it regrets; an honest restore looks the same.
scenarios.fix: Warrants carried by carriers; a lie never voids an ending; a restore starts a new epoch.

proposal.text: Two records with one signer and one running number freeze that signer from the earliest lied-about number; a lie never voids an ending. A warrant (a signed record carrying both conflicting records) travels on the signer's identity topic; carriers check it and refuse the signer's chunks. p2panda's resolver cases become test fixtures.
proposal.why: As written, both conflicting records become invalid, which a signer could use to void a record it regrets.

intents.title: Safe key turns

learn.concept: Keys follow agents; any current reader may turn a key
learn.weakness: Concurrent key turns fork, a counter can't tell them apart, and a turner that hasn't seen a removal leaks its key to the removed reader.
strengths: Read follows the same two layers as write, and removal turns keys; Urbit, Holochain and Autopass don't turn group keys at all.
elsewhere: p2panda's DCGKA picks the latest secret by timestamp, and Secure Scuttlebutt by smallest key, which can be ground.
BeeKEM keeps conflict keys; Distributed MLS gives each member its own sending group, so commits never collide.
Keybase audits that key boxes went to exactly the right members.
Autobase puts the key ID in each block header; Urbit binds key revisions into the encryption.

scenarios.scenario: Two key turns at the same moment
scenarios.why: Future keys reach only readers both allowed, but writers may meanwhile use a key that was sealed to a removed reader.
scenarios.fix: Encrypt only under keys whose recipients are all current readers; otherwise turn first.

proposal.text: A writer encrypts only under a key whose recipients are all among its current readers, otherwise it turns the key first. Among concurrent valid key turns the owner's agent's wins, otherwise the lowest (signer, running number). Key generations are named by a hash of the key turn, with the counter only as a hint. Every key turn is checked for envelope completeness. Chunk headers name the key generation, and the AEAD binds data ID, generation, signer and chunk hash.
proposal.why: Concurrent key turns fork, a counter can't tell them apart, and a turner that hasn't seen a removal leaks its key to the removed reader.

intents.title: Forward-secure envelopes

learn.concept: Keys follow agents; any current reader may turn a key
learn.weakness: Today a stolen agent lock opens every envelope ever sealed to it, meaning all past role keys.
strengths: Read follows the same two layers as write, and removal turns keys; Urbit, Holochain and Autopass don't turn group keys at all.
elsewhere: p2panda's DCGKA picks the latest secret by timestamp, and Secure Scuttlebutt by smallest key, which can be ground.
BeeKEM keeps conflict keys; Distributed MLS gives each member its own sending group, so commits never collide.
Keybase audits that key boxes went to exactly the right members.
Autobase puts the key ID in each block header; Urbit binds key revisions into the encryption.

proposal.text: Agent locks become rotating signed pre-keys with a lifetime, published in the agent's history (as in X3DH). Each envelope also carries fresh key material for the next envelope to that recipient (2SM, from the DCGKA paper), so every lock key is used once.
proposal.why: Today a stolen agent lock opens every envelope ever sealed to it, meaning all past role keys.

intents.title: An invalid add turns keys; envelopes after acknowledgement

learn.concept: Keys follow agents; any current reader may turn a key
learn.weakness: p2panda's leak case at the agent level: the add is dropped, but the newcomer already holds the keys and nothing turns them.
strengths: Read follows the same two layers as write, and removal turns keys; Urbit, Holochain and Autopass don't turn group keys at all.
elsewhere: p2panda's DCGKA picks the latest secret by timestamp, and Secure Scuttlebutt by smallest key, which can be ground.
BeeKEM keeps conflict keys; Distributed MLS gives each member its own sending group, so commits never collide.
Keybase audits that key boxes went to exactly the right members.
Autobase puts the key ID in each block header; Urbit binds key revisions into the encryption.

proposal.text: An add that ends up invalid (made by an agent whose policy was ended at the same moment) counts as a removal for keys: the keys it handed out turn. Newcomers receive envelopes only once their add is acknowledged by the owner's agents.
proposal.why: p2panda's leak case at the agent level: the add is dropped, but the newcomer already holds the keys and nothing turns them.

intents.title: Endings that hold in time

learn.concept: Owner-only endings; time checked on every change
learn.weakness: A holder can sign a time just before expiry and send it later; an owner away in the renewal week locks the household out; no iroh layer revokes anything.
strengths: Readers can no longer end anyone's policy; drops are limited to the ended holder. Stronger than Autobase, where position decides, and Secure Scuttlebutt, which leaves a posting window.
elsewhere: Holochain: an author's times never go backwards along its chain.
Willow: peers reject entries further in the future than the longest capability lifetime.
Matrix: soft fail, not shown or built on, but still part of resolution.
Tlon: the ending is delivered before the session is closed.

scenarios.scenario: A signed time just before the expiry, sent later
scenarios.why: Counts until the owner's lapse arrives; unbounded while the owner is away.
scenarios.fix: Times never fall per signer and must be at least every time in after; a renew-and-lapse-only owner agent.

scenarios.scenario: The owner is offline in the renewal week
scenarios.why: Policies expire; honest writes no longer count and the household is locked out.
scenarios.fix: An always-on owner agent that may only renew and lapse.

proposal.text: A change's signed time must be at least every time in its after and must never fall per signer. An always-on owner agent may only renew and lapse. Far-future records wait instead of being rejected for good. An ending is delivered to the ended agent, then its connections are closed, it is dropped as a neighbour and its transfers are aborted.
proposal.why: A holder can sign a time just before expiry and send it later; an owner away in the renewal week locks the household out; no iroh layer revokes anything.

intents.title: Forgetting safely

learn.concept: Hot, cold, erased, retained
learn.weakness: Back-links stay for 30 days whatever readers have done, and 0-RTT data can be replayed.
strengths: Crypto-shredding goes further than Holochain (never deletes) and Urbit Clay (local tombstones only).
elsewhere: Decentralised MLS deletes an epoch once every member has committed past it.
Clay's tomb and seek: garbage-collect unreferenced data, fetch it again when needed.
Holochain: validation receipts from the peers that store data.

proposal.text: Back-links to older keys are deleted once every reader has acknowledged the newer generation. Values the live state no longer references are garbage-collected within retain rules. Wants and changes on QUIC 0-RTT streams are refused. A keep carrier signs a receipt for each stored chunk before any cut.
proposal.why: Back-links stay for 30 days whatever readers have done, and 0-RTT data can be replayed.

intents.title: A separate network key; no open gossip

learn.concept: Address = signer key; gossip topic = data ID
learn.weakness: iroh needs the raw secret in memory and hands it out, so the signer can't live in an HSM; relays and lookups link every conversation to one ID; iroh-gossip lets anyone who knows a topic join, watch and inject news.
strengths: iroh 1.4 is stable: mutual authentication with raw public keys, hole punching, relays with access control.
elsewhere: Autopass runs its swarm on a separate key pair; Subduction signs its own challenge because its key “may differ from the iroh node identity”.
NextGraph turns topic IDs when it refreshes keys.
iroh-relay's HTTP access callback; iroh's export_keying_material for channel binding.

proposal.text: Each agent gets a network key separate from its signer, certified in its history (“endpoint E acts for agent A until T”) and rotatable on its own. We run our own relay, whose access callback runs theOS checks; address lookup is filled from directory records; mDNS advertising is off or renamed. Gossip topics are replaced by direct subscriptions after a want check; any remaining topic is a keyed hash of data ID and key generation.
proposal.why: iroh needs the raw secret in memory and hands it out, so the signer can't live in an HSM; relays and lookups link every conversation to one ID; iroh-gossip lets anyone who knows a topic join, watch and inject news.

intents.title: Chunk commitments and policy-first sync

learn.concept: Sealed chunks, layers, fingerprints and summaries
learn.weakness: A merged chunk can leave a change out unnoticed, and peers build on changes they will drop later.
strengths: Cost grows with the difference, not the total; compatible with Subduction.
elsewhere: Hypercore: each writer signs a Merkle root over its own log; Autobase syncs by (writer, length) clocks.
Holochain: peers that store data return signed receipts.

scenarios.scenario: A revoked writer, offline, on the same data
scenarios.why: Its changes never listed the ending as seen, so they are dropped everywhere (AIP-60–AIP-62). Until a peer hears the ending, it shows them and may build on them.
scenarios.fix: Policy-first sync, so peers learn endings before chunks.

proposal.text: Each chunk header carries a signed Merkle root over that signer's chunks for the data, so carriers can check gaps and lies without keys. Peers exchange policy, role and ending heads before chunks, and forward warrant pairs first. iroh-blobs moves the bytes behind its request intercept; fingerprints and summaries run on our own ALPN.
proposal.why: A merged chunk can leave a change out unnoticed, and peers build on changes they will drop later.

intents.title: Connection-bound wants and carrier freshness

learn.concept: Carriers see authority, never content
learn.weakness: Stable IDs let a carrier link a person across data; a carrier that hasn't heard an ending keeps serving.
strengths: Stronger than blind peers, which serve anyone who knows a key, forever, and than iroh-blobs, whose requests carry no proof.
elsewhere: Tlon shows join requests and invites only to admins.
Holepunch blind-peering: at least two mirrors chosen by distance to the key, from different operators; quotas and push wake-ups.
iroh-relay binds client auth to the TLS keying material.

scenarios.scenario: A carrier that hasn't heard an ending
scenarios.why: It keeps serving ciphertext and news to the removed holder; content is safe once the key has turned.
scenarios.fix: A freshness bound carried by renewals; endings close connections.

proposal.text: A want is the signer's signature over the connection's exported keying material (label theos/want/1, context the data ID): fresh, bound to the connection, no extra round trip. Records a carrier sees use per-data pseudonyms. A carrier serves only while its newest record from the owner is younger than its own policy's lifetime. Each piece of data lives on at least two carriers from different operators, with quotas and priorities as conditions on keep.
proposal.why: Stable IDs let a carrier link a person across data; a carrier that hasn't heard an ending keeps serving.

intents.title: Ending events and two ways to drop

learn.concept: Owner-only endings; time checked on every change
learn.weakness: Apps would otherwise recompute what an ending removed, and replaying is costly for simple append-only data.
strengths: Readers can no longer end anyone's policy; drops are limited to the ended holder. Stronger than Autobase, where position decides, and Secure Scuttlebutt, which leaves a posting window.
elsewhere: Holochain: an author's times never go backwards along its chain.
Willow: peers reject entries further in the future than the longest capability lifetime.
Matrix: soft fail, not shown or built on, but still part of resolution.
Tlon: the ending is delivered before the session is closed.

proposal.text: For every ending the engine emits the IDs of the changes it invalidates, so apps can show moderation and the conflict view. A schema says how its data drops invalid changes: replayed without them (text, AIP-62) or removed by ID (messages, posts); both converge.
proposal.why: Apps would otherwise recompute what an ending removed, and replaying is costly for simple append-only data.

intents.title: One ordering pipeline; delivery apart from processing

learn.concept: Sealed chunks, layers, fingerprints and summaries
learn.weakness: Today each record kind waits in its own way, and delivery is tied to iroh.
strengths: Cost grows with the difference, not the total; compatible with Subduction.
elsewhere: Hypercore: each writer signs a Merkle root over its own log; Autobase syncs by (writer, length) clocks.
Holochain: peers that store data return signed receipts.

proposal.text: One buffer orders every record kind (policies, endings, key turns, changes) and releases each once its dependencies are in; a logical depth next to the hashes makes concurrency checks cheap. Checking, ordering, decrypting and applying form one pipeline; delivery is pluggable: iroh, carriers, LAN broadcast, or a sealed bundle on a USB stick.
proposal.why: Today each record kind waits in its own way, and delivery is tied to iroh.

intents.title: A message mode with forward secrecy, later

learn.concept: Keys follow agents; any current reader may turn a key
learn.weakness: Data keys give no forward secrecy for content; chats may want it.
strengths: Read follows the same two layers as write, and removal turns keys; Urbit, Holochain and Autopass don't turn group keys at all.
elsewhere: p2panda's DCGKA picks the latest secret by timestamp, and Secure Scuttlebutt by smallest key, which can be ground.
BeeKEM keeps conflict keys; Distributed MLS gives each member its own sending group, so commits never collide.
Keybase audits that key boxes went to exactly the right members.
Autobase puts the key ID in each block header; Urbit binds key revisions into the encryption.

proposal.text: Alongside data keys, where a newcomer may read history, a second mode for chat-like data uses a fresh key per message (a Double Ratchet over the same key agreement), chosen per piece of data.
proposal.why: Data keys give no forward secrecy for content; chats may want it.

intents.title: Records follow schemas too; a root manifest with the meta-schema

decision.text: A record's type is a schema ref (data ID @ version), never a name. Each engine release carries one root manifest: the meta-schema (JSON Schema 2020-12 plus theOS's vocabulary for stored keys and lenses) and one schema version per record kind. The engine trusts exactly those hashes. The meta-schema validates itself, and every schema version, root or not, validates against it. A record whose type isn't in the device's manifest, or reachable from it through lenses, waits. A new manifest keeps old record versions readable through lenses; records are never rewritten.
decision.why: The rule “refer to schemas by data ID and version, never by name” must hold for records too, and something has to check the first schema: a fixed, hash-named root set with a self-validating meta-schema closes the loop.

intents.title: The guardian: every identity's root of trust

learn.concept: Do endings hold?

scenarios.scenario: Two holders below the top remove each other
scenarios.why: Both removals stand; the top repairs, but must come online.

decision.text: Every human and coop has exactly one guardian, its root of trust, kept outside the policy engine. A human's guardian is the ed25519 key PRF(passkey, "theos/guardian"), the same on every device the passkey syncs to and never stored; its agents' signers come from the same passkey with per-device salts (AIP-31). A coop's guardian is exactly one identity, named in its birth record. Every policy on an identity must trace back to its guardian: signed by the guardian, or along a chain of own the guardian gave. own on an identity covers managing its roles, its agents' policies and its data's policies, within the holder's own. The one act reserved to the guardian is changing the guardian: a coop's guardian changes only by a guardian record the current guardian signs, naming its successor and listing the previous record as seen; a guardian can't leave or be removed without a successor, and two concurrent guardian records both fail until one sees the other. Guardian records are checked by the core verifier, like birth records; no policy, condition or plugin can widen, change or remove a guardian. govern is no longer an operation. Agents have no guardian; their owner's guardian stands behind them.
decision.why: One fixed top per identity, so no clash at the top and no lockout, while own still lets the guardian hand all day-to-day management to others. Keeping the root outside the engine makes it small enough to prove things about.
